utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the case for hearing be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-87/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Vlastimir Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning to counsel. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May it please you, I appear along with Ms. Daniela Kravetz and Ms. Priya Gopalan for the Prosecution, and with us, of course, is our case manager, Ms. Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't need each morning, I think, Mr. Stamp to hear the appearance of counsel, but as this is the first day of trial, we will call upon Mr. Djordjevic to announce the counsel appearing in the trial for the Defence. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Defence today is present my co-counsel Mr. Djurdjic and my legal assistants, Ms. Marie O'Leary and Mr. Aleksandar Popovic, as well me personally, as lead counsel, Dragoljub Djordjevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Djordjevic. We welcome all counsel and we look forward to a cooperative, constructive hearing of this trial. We turn now to the opportunity for the Prosecution to make its opening statement. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. At the outset, I should say that the trial commencing today is primarily about the deportation of a substantial proportion of the civilian population of Kosovo. Few of us, I think, can forget the shocking and heart-rending images in the media during 1999 of seemingly endless columns or convoys of refugees, including women, children, the elderly, leaving Kosovo on foot, on animal- and human-drawn carts and wagons, by tractors and any other type of motor vehicle that was available. In all, between the 24th of March, 1999, and the 10th of June, 1999, about 800.000 Kosovar Albanians fled the territory, and that is out of a population of some 2 million, a little over 2 million. They fled to the neighbouring states, primarily Albania and Macedonia. Most of them departed in the first month of the conflict. This trial is about how and why that human exodus from Kosovo took place and about who was responsible for it. The Prosecution says that the evidence in this case will show that the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic, participated with other members of the Serbian political, military, and police leadership in a joint criminal enterprise, a JCE as we call it, to expel a significant portion of the Kosovo Albanian population from Kosovo, and that the execution of this plan involved terrorising the Kosovo Albanian population into fleeing by the commission of many acts of persecution against them, including and in particular murder. The purpose of the JCE, the joint criminal enterprise, was to modify the ethnic balance of Kosovo in order to maintain and continue Serbian control over the province. While motive is not a necessary element for us to prove in this case, it is a factor that can help Your Honours to understand the evidence. Thus you will hear some evidence about the special importance of Kosovo in Serbian history and its importance to some members of the leadership of the Serbian government. And I should tell you here that I will probably, in the course of this opening address, use acronyms, fall into the habits of using acronyms, like JCE for joint criminal enterprise. I have distributed and I hope Your Honours have in your possession a glossary of the common acronyms for various organs, organisations and persons -- not persons, but organisations relevant to this case. I think it has been delivered to Your Honours. In furtherance of the objective of the JCE, the authors of this campaign of ethnic cleansing executed a concerted plan to terrorise the ethnic Albanians into leaving the province. You will hear evidence of massive executions and the systematic process by which Serbian forces went from hamlet to hamlet, village to village, town to town, murdering, raping, burning, looting and destroying property in their path. And it will be readily perceived by the end of the Prosecution's case that the massive movement of refugees throughout Kosovo and out of Kosovo was a direct consequence of the rampages of these forces. This process had the intended effect of frightening the civilian population to leave their homes. Villagers could hear the sound of artillery from neighbouring villages, see houses burning, hear horror stories from fleeing victims and feared that the same fate awaited them. Consequently, many of them would load their families on carts or tractors or any means of transport available and join the convoys to avoid being beaten, raped, or even murdered. The looting and burning and destruction of Kosovo Albanian property was intended to ensure that there was nothing left for them to return to, if they dared. So as I indicated, the main issue in this case is deportation but also the principal means employed to achieve the deportation and that is murder. Before discussing the crimes and the perpetrators, I think it would be useful, Your Honours, if I gave a brief overview in the area that we are discussing, its demographics, population, and people. It might be useful to show a couple of maps in talking about the history of Kosovo. During the trial you may hear it referred to in a variety of ways. We here will call it Kosovo, sometimes Kosovo and Metohija. If you ever look at the first map, I think, on your screens, this is a map of the Balkans showing the various states surrounding Serbia and Kosovo, in the whole scheme of things. I don't know if Your Honours have it on your screens. I think if you hit the video button --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We each have the display, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the wars of the early 1990s, the former Yugoslavia, then called the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY, looked like the picture you're seeing on the screen. The SFRY was then made up of six republics. In alphabetical order, they are Bosnia, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Slovenia. Within Serbia itself were the two so-called autonomous provinces of Vojvodina to the north and Kosovo to the south. As you can see, Kosovo was located to the south and importantly its southern border, its south-west border, was shared with Albania; and that is an important factor, I think, to remember in the geography when we come to deal with evidence with the movements of people and the development of the joint criminal enterprise in this case. Kosovo had been contested territory for much of its history. Between 1912 and 1918, and again during World War II, Kosovo was occupied by a number of different invaders. At the end of the Second World War, Kosovo was formally annexed to Serbia. You will find that Kosovo is a very small area, geographically speaking, notwithstanding its population of 2 million people. And if we look at the next map on the screen, you will see the main towns of Kosovo. Many of these towns are the towns that will be the subject -- or we will discuss in terms of being the locations where many of the crimes charged in the indictment were committed. You will see the capital of the province, Pristina, toward the centre but to the right, that is, to the east of the province. Kosovo is barely 150 kilometres at its widest point, and some inferences can be drawn from the size of the place. If you -- I would like to show you another map. This is a map with the 29 municipalities of Kosovo. The deportation counts and indeed the murder counts are organised in terms of the municipalities in which they occurred. This map simply shows the municipalities, and no doubt as the case progresses, Your Honours, you will become more familiar with the relevant municipalities in the case. You will note that in the indictment and in some maps that you will be shown in the process of -- in the course of the case, there will be alternative spellings for the place names, with the Serbian version first followed by the Albanian. In certain instances, the name is the same in both languages. Some witnesses, mainly the Serbian witnesses, will refer to the Serbian names and the Albanian witnesses will probably refer to the Albanian names. We will use the Serbian names to ensure that the accused and his representatives know where we're talking about. The population of Kosovo, if we could turn to the demographics, was composed of two groups - Albanians and Serbs. Prior to the conflict in 1999, the last census, with nearly complete participation, took place in 1981 and showed a total population for Kosovo of approximately 1.585 million citizens, that is 1 million, 585.000 citizens, of which 77 percent were Albanians, and 13 percent were Serbs. The remaining 10 percent consisted of different groups, including Roma and Turks, that were smaller in number. The next census in 1991 was boycotted by Kosovo Albanians, but the general estimates of the Kosovo population in 1998 suggest that the total population for Kosovo in that year was in the neighbourhood of between 2 and 2.2 million people, of which Kosovo Albanians constituted 80 to 85 percent, and Serbs approximately 10 percent. So you will see a change in the demographics, declining proportion of Serbs and increasing proportion of ethnic Albanians in the population. And we intend to lead expert evidence on the demographic composition of the population at the relevant time. All the crimes charged in the indictment against the accused, the persecutions, which includes the rapes, physical assaults, robbery, destruction of property, and the murders, occurred during the first half of 1999. However, the indictment also alleges specifically that in 1998 forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is the FRY, and of Serbia had engaged in conduct involving excessive and indiscriminate force and attacks against civilians. This is important background for understanding what happened later, not least of all how the joint criminal enterprise developed and to gain some insight into the state of mind of the accused Djordjevic and his awareness that forces subordinated to him had and were likely to commit crimes against Kosovo Albanian civilians when they came in contact with them. And so for a better understanding of the events in that first half of 1999, I propose to give a very brief overview of the history of the area of Kosovo and its place in the nation, the Serbian state. In 1974, a new constitution was passed in the SFRY, that's the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which in effect provided for a shift of power from the central federal authority to the six constituent republics, that is, Bosnia, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Slovenia, and to the two provinces, the two autonomous provinces of Vojvodina and Kosovo which were part of Serbia. The powers granted included republican and provincial control over the judiciary, the police, and the educational system. So we see at that point a devolution of power towards the province of Kosovo. In 1980 President Tito, who had led Yugoslavia for 35 years, died. Shortly after that, ethnic and nationalistic fears long suppressed were given vent. Political unrest began to stir in Kosovo. In the 1980s, the Kosovo Serbs voiced their concerns about discrimination against them by the Albanian majority provincial government. Meanwhile, during the same period of the 1980s, Kosovo Albanians expressed concern about economic underdevelopment in the province. The Kosovo Albanians also sought additional political liberalisation and republic status for Kosovo. Beginning in the 1980s and continuing on and through the 1990s, Kosovo Albanians frequently staged demonstrations in support of greater independence and autonomy, which were often forcibly suppressed by the military and police forces of Serbia. In 1989, in particular the SFRY Presidency responded strongly to the ongoing unrest in Kosovo, declaring that the situation had deteriorated to such an extent as to threaten the constitution, integrity, and sovereignty of the country. The SFRY Presidency imposed special measures which reassigned police authority and responsibility for public security from the provincial government of Kosovo back to the federal government of the SFRY. So we see a reversal of the constitutional process or the constitutional achievements of 1974 underway. On the 23rd of March, 1989, the Kosovo Assembly met, and we say, and you'll hear evidence from the first witness, I believe, we say that under threat and duress and intimidation, caused in no small part by the presence of tanks outside the Assembly building, the members voted to give up control of the police, education, choice of official language, and veto powers over further changes to the Serbian constitution. A few days later the Assembly of Serbia approved changes to the constitution and revoked the autonomy previously granted to Kosovo in 1974. The courts and municipal councils in Kosovo ceased to function. Not surprisingly there followed more strikes, more demonstrations, and more agitation by the populous of Kosovo in support of the autonomy and independence, and these actions were strongly suppressed by the Serbian authorities. In the early 1990s, measures were put in place that we say were the early attempts by legislative means to alter the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serbian control of the province. By then it was seen that the province was slipping away, and the major factor which impeded Serbian control was the fact of the minority status and the declining proportion of the population. Albanian professionals were removed from their jobs merely because of their ethnicity, and they were replaced by Serbs whether qualified for the position or not. Indeed, after the outbreak of war in Croatia and Bosnia, a significant number of Serbian refugees from those republics were relocated to Kosovo in order to bolster the Serbian population there, and special incentives to lure Serbs to settle in Kosovo were attempted. But this particular sort of effort to alter the ethnic balance in favour of the Serbs did not meet with any great success. In July 1999 -- in July 1990, the Kosovo Assembly passed an unofficial resolution declaring Kosovo to be an equal and independent entity within the SFRY, that is, equal to the republics of Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia. The Assembly of Serbia responded within a matter of days by passing a decision suspending or dissolving the Assembly of Kosovo. The suspended Kosovo Assembly continued to remain active, however, and in September 1990 proclaimed a constitution for the would-be "Republic of Kosovo." This is what they called it. A year later, in September 1991, the Kosovo Albanians held an unofficial referendum which was overwhelmingly in favour of independence. In May 1992 the Kosovo Albanians held official elections for an assembly -- sorry, held unofficially elections. They had been officially dissolved by the Serbian parliament. They held unofficial elections for the Assembly and president for their own "Republic of Kosovo," as they called it. Ibrahim Rugova, now deceased, a founder and member of the Democratic League of Kosovo was chosen president and six years later was re-elected to that position. During the early 1990s, the LDK, as I would call the Democratic League of Kosovo, the LDK led an unofficial coalition government and pursued a policy of a non-violent civil resistance and began establishing unofficial parallel institutions in the sectors of education and health care in Kosovo. So the early 1990s, was a period when the majority Kosovo Albanians kept up the pressure in asserting their desire for greater independence or autonomy by acts of protests or acts of civil disobedience, and the Serbian authorities responded by restricting or removing whatever authority and power they had, and sometimes with violence. By the mid 1990s, there was growing dissolution on the part of Kosovo Albanians with Dr. Rugova and the LDK's policy of non-violent resistance, and a faction of Kosovo Albanians organised a group known as Ushtria Clirimtare e Kosoves. Notwithstanding that I've practiced this, I'm sure I didn't get it right. But this group, the UCK - or as it is known in English, and this is what we're call it because it's easier to say, the Kosovo Liberation Army - exposed a contrary position to Dr. Rugova's LDK. The Kosovo Liberation Army advocated a policy of armed insurgency and violent resistance to the Serb authorities in Kosovo. The KLA began launching armed attacks, primarily against the Serbian police forces in the mid and latter part of the 1990s. The Serbian police responded forcefully with numerous operations against suspected KLA bases and supporters in Kosovo, and the persecution of Kosovo Albanians -- Albanian civilians became more common and widespread. The alternating pattern of aggression by the KLA on the one hand and the responses of the forces of the FRY and Serbia on the other continued throughout 1997 and 1998 with an ever-increasing cycle of violence. And if I may pause just to touch upon two matters. First, regarding use of the term "forces of the FRY and Serbia." This is a term that's been defined in the indictment. It's a term to include not only units of the army of the FRY, the Yugoslav Army or the VJ, as we will call it from time to time, and of the Ministry of the Interior, that is, the police, but also various military, territorial units, civil defence units, village defence forces, which were armed locals, locals armed by the police and VJ, and volunteer units attached to and assigned to or otherwise incorporated into the VJ or the MUP. So it's an all-embracing term. Secondly, I will just say from early that the Prosecution readily accepts that grave crimes, very grave crimes, were committed by members of the KLA against the Serbian civilians, the police and other ethnic groups, including Kosovo Albanians who were loyal to the Serbian state. Indeed, the OTP has proffered indictments against several of the members of the KLA for these offences. This case is about the other side of the coin, the crimes committed by the forces of the FRY and Serbia against the Kosovo Albanian civilians. Any attempt by the accused to justify his conduct or that of the forces under his command on the grounds that offences of a similar character may have been committed against civilians by another party to the conflict has no basis, it is submitted, in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. At the beginning of 1996 and 1997, the KLA was a small, poorly armed and disorganised group. Most of its leadership was abroad. But due in part to the availability of additional weapons following a collapse of law and order in neighbouring Albania at about that time, and an ever-growing number of volunteers, the KLA in 1998 grew to include several thousand members and to become more and more active against the Serb police. Indeed, it, by 1998, controlled significant parts of the territory of Kosovo. And not only were actions directed against the police but also against Kosovo Albanians, as I said before, loyal to the Serb authorities. So the conflict intensified, and the Serb response to KLA activities was widely viewed as being disproportionate and amounting to excessive and indiscriminate force against Kosovo Albanian civilians. Villages and towns where there were KLA positions were shelled and the residents were driven away. The problem was significant enough by then to gain international attention. Significantly, in March 1998, Serb forces carried out an operation in the Srbica municipality, attacking the family compound of a notable KLA activist, one Adem Jashari, in the village of Donji Prekaz, killing over 50 people, including Jashari and his entire family, except for an 11-year-old girl. Now, in using the word "compound," or "family compound," the expression "family compound," I am describing a particular feature of Kosovo Albanian architecture that you will hear more about in the course of the trial. It's the fairly common practice of different family units that are part of one extended family, sometimes of several generations, living in separate houses built within one family compound that it supports sounded by a wall. It doesn't mean that the Jashari family compound was a military fortification of some sort. And I will also add that it is doubtless that several persons on the compound had been involved in KLA activity. However, the brutal, excessive, and indiscriminate nature of the assault shocked the conscience of many observers, both local and international. In March 1998, the United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 1160 which condemned, and I quote, "the excessive --" sorry, may I begin again, quote, "the excessive use --" I will start over the quote. Quote: "The use of excessive force by the Serbian police forces against civilians and peaceful demonstrators in Kosovo." This resolution will be put in evidence. It's the Prosecution's submission that the accused, as chief of the police, was aware of the excessive force and aware of the international condemnation of it. The resolution also condemned the violence, indiscriminate violence, by the KLA. Despite the March 1998 United Nations resolution condemning their practices, the forces of the FRY and Serbia not only continued with their operations against the KLA, including against the civilian population in areas where KLA operated, but increased the ferocity and intensity of that campaign. In July 1998, the forces of the FRY and Serbia began a large-scale offensive throughout the entire province of Kosovo. The operation included among others various brigades of the VJ's Pristina Corps and special units of the MUP. It is interesting to note here that the month before the launch of this big summer offensive we see the creation of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, as it was known, and which will play an important role in future operations in Kosovo, and it will we discussed a little further on. The mandate of the Joint Command was to coordinate civil affairs and activities and also coordinate the activities of the police and the army when they're engaged in operations in Kosovo. The Joint Command had no official role or legitimacy in Serbian law or the constitution, but its role and importance is reflected by a VJ military order dated the 7th of July, 1998, from the commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade, declaring a ban on all operations without the knowledge and approval of the Joint Command. So this unofficial ad hoc body, of which the accused was a member, was involved in and responsible for coordinating the activities of the security forces in Kosovo in 1998. The Joint Command meetings occurred on almost a daily basis during the big offensive from July to October 1998, and the accused regularly attended meetings, along with some of his former co-accused, Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic. We expect that the evidence led in respect to the events of 1998 and the accused's role and statements he made at Joint Command meetings will show that he was aware of the excessive and indiscriminate force directed against Kosovar Albanian civilians by forces of the FRY and Serbia, including the police for whom he was responsible. We will tender minutes of these meetings where the discussion of the use of excessive force was commonplace, and we will at the appropriate stage submit that it shows that he was aware of the likelihood that the forces that he commanded would commit crimes of the nature that are charged. In the face of this continuing campaign of disproportionate force of the civilian population in Kosovo, the United Nations Security Council adopted another resolution on the 23rd of September, 1998. This was Resolution 1199 and it called for an immediate cease-fire in Kosovo, an international presence to monitor that cease-fire, and the withdrawal of security forces used for civilian repression. This resolution and the increasing outcry on both the domestic and international fronts forced the FRY government to engage in international negotiations in 1998. You will hear some detailed evidence about those negotiations which occurred. These talks resulted in a number of agreements, the so-called October Agreements, signed by the representatives of the FRY, Serbia, NATO, and the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe. The accused was one of the key participants from the Serbian side on behalf of the police, during the course of these negotiations. Key provisions insisted upon by the international interlocutors were the cessation of the use of excessive and indiscriminate force against the civilian population and the reduction of VJ and MUP forces in Kosovo. The agreement also called for the creation and deployment of a verification mission from the OSCE to be called the Kosovo Verification Mission, which consisted of unarmed observers deployed in the province to verify compliance with the terms of the agreement. And you will hear testimony from several of these members as to what transpired after the coming into force of these agreements. It is to be noted that a United Nations report found that by the end of October 1998, approximately 285.000 Kosovo Albanians had been displaced from their homes, either internally in Kosovo, some camping out in mountains, forests, fields, and in other villages; and some had been displaced across the border into neighbouring countries. And one should note here the early estimates of the population, 285.000 persons out of the Kosovo Albanian population amounts approximately one in six persons being forced out of their homes in 1998, and this was highlighted by the international community and must have been within the awareness of the accused, who was one of the leading Serbian negotiators with the international community. The October Agreements, unfortunately, did not achieve the hoped-for results. There was some initially withdrawals of Serb forces in the beginning. However, the KLA quickly moved in to fill the void in those areas and remained active against forces of the FRY and Serbia. By December, the numbers of Serb forces were on the rise again. From their arrival in November 1998 until their departure in March 1999, the KVM observers noted in addition to operations against the KLA there was ongoing violence by forces of the FRY and Serbia against the civilian population. This included an operation in January 1999 in the area of Racak, which left 40 Kosovar Albanians dead, and that event helped spur the ongoing efforts to stop the violence in Kosovo. There were international meetings, including an international peace conference in Rambouillet in Paris, France, in March 1999. During these negotiations the fighting in Kosovo continued. The Rambouillet negotiations, I should say, were in February 1999. The talks eventually collapsed in Paris in mid-March 1999. With the failure of the negotiations, the KVM verifiers withdraw from Kosovo. On the 23rd of March, 1999, a declaration of an imminent threat of war was proclaimed by the FRY. The next day, the 24th of March, 1999, the NATO bombing campaign began in Kosovo and elsewhere in Serbia and the FRY parliament declared a state of war. So we see over the period of 1990s increasing violence and increasing determination on the KLA side by acts of violence, often illegal and criminal, to dislodge the Serbian state from Kosovo and the violent responses by the Serbian authorities. It was by then becoming clear that drastic measures had to be taken in order to resolve the Kosovo issue. And from early as February 1999, members of the JCE had already begun planning the joint police and VJ operations which were later undertaken in order to achieve their aim of modifying the ethnic balance under the guise of crushing the KLA. We will see that the accused was integrally involved in the planning of these operations. When the opportunity arose, the members of the JCE acted by launching large-scale joint operations using the forces of the FRY and Serbia. The JCE's objective of modifying the ethnic balance to maintain Serbian control in the province, that is, by depopulating Kosovo of a significant proportion of the Albanians living there, was largely achieved by the end of April, although some more isolated operations continued to occur after this. Who were the major players in this drama? The evidence will show that many of the important leaders in the Serbian and Yugoslav state played a part in bringing into effect this JCE. Of course, first and foremost for the purposes of this trial is the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic, whose formal position is set out in detail in the indictment and the pre-trial brief. At the material time he was posted at the MUP headquarters in Belgrade as an Assistant Minister of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, and he was chief of the Public Security Department of the police, that is, the regular uniformed police side of the MUP. There was another department in the MUP, the State Security Department, called the RDB, which was akin to a secret service involving intelligence-gathering. We'll talk more about these departments later on when we discuss the MUP. But suffice it to say for now that as Chief of the Public Security Department of the MUP, that is, the RJB, the accused Djordjevic had overall responsibility for and exercised control over the police units on the ground in Kosovo that participated in committing the crimes charged in this indictment. He reported directly to the Minister of Interior, that is, Mr. Stojiljkovic. Mr. Djordjevic had originally been indicted with six others who we say were also participants in the joint criminal enterprise: Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, Dragoljub Ojdanic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Vladimir Lazarevic, and Sreten Lukic. But before I come to briefly describing who they were and what their positions were, may I start, it is convenient I think to start from the top. Slobodan Milosevic, who should be on the screen now. No account - no account - of the conflict in Kosovo in 1999 could be told without mentioning him. He was the President of the FRY, the undisputed leader, and without question the most powerful individual in the country at the time the crimes alleged in the indictment were committed. His role in the JCE was that of the paramount leader, the one who gave orders, the primary planner and instigator. Milosevic surrounded himself with loyal followers who shared his views about the importance of Kosovo to Serbia and who could be relied upon to take the necessary actions to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serbian control in the province. He was not only the President of the FRY but he was also the President of the most powerful political party in Serbia at the time, the SPS, and thus had significant de jure and de facto ability to affect and control operations within the various organs of government, the military, and the police. Next is Milan Milutinovic, a former co-indictee of the accused. Milutinovic was a high-ranking member of the SPS and a close associate of Slobodan Milosevic. He was President of Serbia, one of the constituent states of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from December 1997 until December 2002. The other state in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I should mention, at that time was Montenegro. As President of Serbia, Milutinovic was one of the three voting members of the Supreme Defence Council, an important body that was responsible for organising security of the country. Milutinovic's prominent position as President of Serbia, as a member of the SDC and the Supreme Command, together with his close association with Milosevic and his high status in the SPS, the party in power, combined to give him substantial de jure power and de facto influence and control over the army, the police, and other organs and individuals engaged in implementing the objectives of the JCE. Nikola Sainovic is the next. By all accounts he was an even closer confidante of Milosevic and considered part of Milosevic's inner circle. From 1994 to 2000 he held the post of Deputy Prime Minister of the FRY. In 1998 and 1999, Sainovic was Milosevic's personal choice to be delegated with primary responsibility for Kosovo matters. He was also head of the Joint Command and he exercised authority and control over the forces of the FRY and Serbia operating on the ground in Kosovo in his capacity as head of the Joint Command. Three of the accused Djordjevic's co-indictees were commanders of the Yugoslav Army, the VJ. The VJ acted in coordination with the police in the commission of many of the crimes charged in the indictment. It was a modern professional army which, in acting in coordination with other elements of the forces of the FRY in Serbia, played a vital role in the implementation of the JCE. If we briefly look down the chain of command from the top, I should point out first that the constitution of the FRY and federal legislation provided that the overall command of the VJ was the FRY president, then Milosevic. Below him you'll see on your screen General Dragoljub Ojdanic. He was appointed Chief of the General Staff of the VJ by Milosevic on the 24th of November, 1998, and remained in that position during the indictment period. As Chief of the VJ's General Staff, he was the highest ranking, most authoritative officer in the VJ, and exercised the highest professional military level of command and effective control over the three services of the VJ - the land forces, the air and air defence forces, and the navy. Below him in the chain of command was General Nebojsa Pavkovic. The land forces of the VJ, specifically the Third Army then under the control of General Pavkovic, is most relevant to the events in Kosovo in 1999. Pavkovic was appointed Commander of the Third Army on the 25th of December, 1998, and remained in that post throughout 1999. He was also a member of the Joint Command of Kosovo in 1998 and 1999. Kosovo was the area of responsibility of a unit of the Third Army known as the Pristina Corps, and the Pristina Corps was commanded by General Vladimir Lazarevic, who you will see coming up on your screen now. He was appointed Commander of the Pristina Corps on the 25th of December, 1998. He was also an active member of and participated in the Joint Command in Kosovo. In this particular trial, you will probably be more interested in the role of the MUP and its leadership, this accused being a former senior commander thereof. And so I come to the sixth co-indictee, or former co-indictee of the accused, that is, Sreten Lukic. From June 1998 throughout 1999, Lukic was head of the MUP Staff in Kosovo. We will hear a little bit more on the MUP Staff later on. As such he was the highest ranking MUP official posted in Kosovo. He commanded MUP operations in Kosovo and was also a member and participant in the meetings and decision-making of the Joint Command. As head of the MUP Staff for Kosovo, Sreten Lukic exercised command authority and effective control over MUP units deployed in Kosovo and those units subordinated to the MUP for operations in Kosovo. He was a direct subordinate of the accused Djordjevic. Other senior MUP officials of interest include Vlajko Stojiljkovic, now deceased. He was a Minister of Internal Affairs of Serbia at the material time. We allege that he was a member of the JCE, and his name will be mentioned often in the course of this trial. As the Minister of Internal affairs, he was the political head of the MUP and had responsibility for the work of the MUP and its personnel during the time-frame of this indictment. We will also hear a lot about Obrad Stevanovic, who was an assistant Minister of Police who headed the Police Administration, a sub-division of the Public Security Division. He was frequently on the ground in Kosovo during the indictment period, coordinating the operations of special units of the MUP. And he again is someone that you will hear mentioned quite often in the course of this trial. Next, Radomir Markovic. He was also an Assistant Minister of the MUP, on the same level of the accused Djordjevic. The MUP, as I indicated earlier, had two branchs: the Public Security Division, that's the RJB, and the State Security Division, the RDB. The State Security Division was headed by Markovic, and it was primarily involved in performing the task of collecting information and intelligence relating to state security of the Republic of Serbia. If we could take a closer look at the organisation of the MUP with a chart which I wish to put before you. This is the organisation of the MUP in so far as it relates to Kosovo. The Ministry of the Interior was mandated by Serbian law to protect human lives and the safety of persons and their possessions and to maintain law and order. The RJB side of the MUP, that's public security side of the MUP, that Djordjevic was chief of, comprised of the ordinary uniformed police who did regular day-to-day police work of crime-prevention, investigation, enforcement of traffic laws, border control, and the normal operation of the police. I think that the Court could take particular note that the police involved in border control were under the supervision or were subordinated to this accused. We will see that in respect to the deportation offences, what happened at the borders and the conduct of the police at the borders was of great importance. In addition to the police officers conducting normal police work, the RJB also had special units which were heavily armed and specially trained and equipped to conduct operations, including combat, which could not be done by the regular police. Witnesses will tell you that these police were often armed with armoured personnel carriers, mortars, grenades, and other weapons we might not normally associate with the police. In Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, the following special units of the RJB were actively engaged: The main special unit was called, simply, the Special Police Units, or the PJP, as we'll hear it being referred to quite frequently. There's also the Operational Sweep Groups, or the OPGs. And the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, or the SAJ, which was a highly elite combat unit of the police. The state security side of the MUP which the accused controlled also -- I'm sorry. The state security side of the MUP was controlled by Markovic, Radomir Markovic, and that side controlled a special unit of its own which was engaged also in operations in Kosovo. This was called the Special Operations Unit. Most witnesses, particularly police officers, will refer to it by its acronym, the JSO. On the chart you'll see that all of these units fell under the MUP Staff for Kosovo, and many of these units, you'll hear from the evidence, were involved in much of the activities resulting in the crimes that were committed against the Kosovo Albanian population. These units reported up to the accused through the MUP Staff in Kosovo, headed by Lukic, and they reported up to the accused sometimes directly. We intend to tender several orders issued by the accused deploying these units or personnel of these units in Kosovo which we say demonstrate his overall command role over these units as chief of the RJB. For example, one of the dispatches we intend to bring before the Court is one of the accused of the 21st of March, 1999, where he deployed a company of PJPs from Subotica in Serbia proper to the 23rd PJP detachment in Kosovo. This was on the 21st of March, 1999. The unit deployed was actively engaged in operations in the Orahovac municipality. This is where Bela Crkva and Mala Krusa are located, and we will hear in evidence of the massacres that were committed there in those two villages by the police on the 25th of March. So the accused had overall responsibility for all these police units operating in Kosovo. In addition to all this, the MUP had reservists to supplement its regular contingent. MUP reservists formed the core of local defence units established in many parts of Kosovo. Within Kosovo province, the standard work of MUP was divided on a geographical basis. If we could go back to the graphic, the chart, we'll see at the bottom of the chart the seven separate regional secretariats of the interior, as they were called, and often in this case they'll be referred to merely as SUPs by some of the witnesses, each responsible for RJB tasks in the municipalities making up Kosovo provinces. So the SUPs would be the police headquarters governing several municipalities in Kosovo. The SUPs, shown at the bottom of the chart, reported up the chain of command, sometimes through the Joint Command, sometimes through the MUP Staff for Kosovo, and sometimes directly to the MUP headquarters in Belgrade. If we can look at the seven -- you will see the seven areas or geographic areas in Kosovo where these SUPs were organisationally responsible for. And the next map will show the municipalities that was covered in each of these regions by the seven SUPs in Kosovo. In addition to the role of the SUPs, you will hear much evidence in this case about the role of command and control organs over the forces of the FRY and Serbia, particularly the MUP Staff for Kosovo and Metohija and the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. The MUP Staff for Kosovo was located in Pristina and from June 1998 through to June 1999 was headed by Sreten Lukic. Its purpose was to manage and coordinate the work of the MUP on the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo and to organise and direct the work of the MUP units when performing more complex security tasks in the province. The MUP Staff in Kosovo included RDB members, as well as the department heads in Kosovo and also the chiefs of the seven regional SUPs in Kosovo. As head of the MUP Staff for Kosovo, in 1998 Lukic was required to report to the Minister of Internal Affairs, Stojiljkovic. He also reported to the accused Djordjevic, his immediate superior. Daily situation reports went to, among others, the minister, the assistant minister, including this accused as head of the RJB. And as I pointed out, in addition to these regular daily reports, the seven regional SUPs were required to report significant events not only to the MUP Staff in Pristina but also directly to the MUP headquarters in Belgrade. This reporting regime was supplemented by the fact that MUP higher-ups, such as the minister himself, the accused Djordjevic, and the Head of Police Administration Obrad Stevanovic sometimes attended meetings of the MUP Staff in Kosovo. I have already made mention of the Joint Command. I should just pause here to point out and to alert you to the existence of another body that was sometimes referred to as the Joint Command. During 1998 and 1999 in Belgrade, there existed an ad hoc body composed of high-ranking military, political, and police officials that met and discussed matters relating to the events and actions in Kosovo. The participants included Milosevic, Sainovic, Ojdanic, Pavkovic, and the accused Djordjevic, and sometimes Minister Stojiljkovic. This body had no apparent basis in law nor an official title. In addition to Joint Command, it was sometimes referred to as the "State Commission" or the "Inter-Departmental Staff for the Suppression of Terrorism." This group that met in Belgrade is to be distinguished from the Joint Command of Kosovo and Metohija, which met in Kosovo, in Pristina. When we, the Prosecution, use the term "Joint Command," we will be talking about the body in Kosovo, and references to the Belgrade group will be specifically noted in a fashion so that they can be distinguished. If I could turn now, Your Honours, with your leave, to the crimes alleged. The accused is charged with persecutions, forced transfers, deportations, and murders committed in the first half of 1999 in Kosovo. The evidence will show that at the material time there was an ongoing armed conflict in Kosovo, at first between the forces of the FRY and Serbia on the one hand and the KLA on the other hand; later between the forces of the FRY and Serbia on the one hand and NATO and the KLA on the other. During this conflict thousands of Kosovo Albanian civilians and non-combatants were killed by forces of the FRY and Serbia. As many as 800.000 were forcibly transferred and deported. That, Your Honours, is one out of three of the total population of Kosovo and one out of two of the Kosovo Albanian population of Kosovo. You know, Your Honours, from the indictment, the pre-trial brief, and my earlier comments of chronology leading up to 1999 that the crimes in 1999 are just the final chapter in a campaign of persecutions and executing violence engaged in by the forces of FRY and Serbia and their leaders to try and maintain physical and political control of the province of Kosovo in the face of ever-growing demands by the Kosovo Albanian majority for increasing autonomy and independence. In only one week between the 24th of March, 1999 and the 30th of March, 1999, United Nations data reflect that some 94.000 Kosovars fled Albania. Many reported that they did not know where their men were as they had been separated from them at the time they were expelled. That will be a common theme in the expulsions. Many reported that they had been deliberately expelled and explicitly told to leave and that their homes had been destroyed by Serb forces. Many reported that they had to leave on little or no notice at all, forced to flee at night, on foot, in freezing temperatures, often with nothing more than the clothes on their backs and whatever few things they could grab to carry in their hands as they rushed out of the door. Many reported having been rounded up by Serb forces and put on trains or buses to be taken to the border for expulsion to Albania or Macedonia. Your Honours, if I could at this brief moment preface my comments by showing a video of one of these convoys, without any sound, and I think it should not take too long, perhaps a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We submit, Your Honours, that the vast majority of these refugees fled because of actions of the VJ, the MUP, and other forces of the FRY and Serbia. From the 24th of March, 1999, following the evacuation of the KVM monitors and the onset of the NATO bombing campaign, the forces of the FRY and Serbia seized the moment to step up their campaign of ethnic cleansing. All across Kosovo, in a concerted and coordinated manner, the forces of the FRY and Serbia began their widespread and systematic attack on the Kosovo Albanian civilian population, forcing them out of Kosovo. The evidence will show that a typical pattern occurred in many municipalities. The Serb forces -- the Serbian forces would nearly -- would encircle a village or town and leave one avenue of escape. The VJ would commence shelling with artillery and heavy weapons. Then MUP units, including special units and volunteers incorporated into the MUP or otherwise attached to the MUP, would enter the town, force the people out, sometimes killing and raping as they did so, often looting and burning the abandoned homes. As I said, the destruction of the homes was to ensure that the expelled population would have nothing to return to. And this type of activity understandably created an atmosphere of terror, and the inhabitants of neighbouring villages, seeing this happen and hearing the stories of the primary victims, would join in fleeing to avoid the same fate happening to them. And so we saw those massive convoys in the international media at the end of March 1999, as thousands and thousands, hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanian civilians literally fled for their lives. Of particular note on this point, you will hear evidence of many of the witnesses, many of the refugees, about how on route out of the country and at the border forces of the FRY and Serbia, including the border police, regularly forced them to hand over their identity documents and vehicle licence plates and leave them behind. Now, why should these people be forced to hand over their identity documents? We suggest that this is a clear manifestation of the objective of the JCE to modify the ethnic balance of Kosovo in order to maintain Serbian control. Once outside of the country and with no official identity documents, these refugees would have severe difficulties if they ever attempted to return to Kosovo, as the Serb authorities could simply claim that they were illegal immigrants. The indictment reflects the widespread nature of this campaign. It includes 11 killing sites and 13 deportation sites. I'd like to note at this point that the crimes that are specifically detailed in the indictment are arranged according to established offences, such as deportation or murder. That's really a breakdown for the purposes of facilitating analysis of individual crimes in the indictment rather than necessarily reflecting any divergence between the deportations and the murders on the ground. So when we see references to deportation sites and references to killing sites, this is not to suggest that they are separate offences or separate events. They are integrated, obviously. Before and during the deportations, killings occurred as well. Further, the 11 killing sites and 13 deportation sites are not a complete list of all the crimes reported to investigators but rather these were selected as a representative sample sufficient, we think, to show the existence of a pattern and to reflect the scope and nature of the campaign conducted throughout the province. Now, if we could look at the criminal sites generally on the screen. These are the killing sites as reflected in the indictment. The witnesses whose evidence we propose to adduce in respect to these sites and these murders are the fortunate ones. They escaped with their lives. Many of their relatives, sometimes their entire families, their neighbours, did not survive the expulsion campaign to tell the tale. Their stories will have to be told by the ones who did survive and also from the grave by the evidence of forensic pathologist, forensic anthropologists, and DNA experts who sedulously analysed bits of human remains, bone, fabric, and identification documents during months and years of exhumations all over Kosovo and other burial sites in Serbia proper. I will go through some of not all of them in order to give you a sketch of the pattern of what happened in many of these murder sites and how the evidence fits together. If we could look first at Bela Crkva, just to identify where that is in Kosovo, towards the south, perhaps the south-west, and this is in the municipality of Orahovac, one of the municipalities where many of the crimes, some not recounted in the indictment, but many crimes against the Kosovo Albanian population occurred, in that municipality. At the village of Bela Crkva, on the 25th of March, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked the villagers. Many of the villagers fled along a small river and hid under a railroad bridge. Serbian police opened fire on one group of villagers heading for the bridge, killing about 12 people, ten of whom were women and children. The remaining villagers were ordered out of the stream-bed and from under the bridge. The men and older boys were separated, ordered to strip and then robbed of their valuables and identity documents. The women and children were ordered to leave to another nearby village. The village doctor tried to intercede with the police commander, but he and his nephew were shot and killed on the spot. The remaining boys and men were then ordered back into the stream-bed. The Serbian forces, the police then opened fire, killing some 65 of them. Some survived and lived to tell the tale. This is a theme that you will see in many situations because these were large massacres. Many times persons survived. The village itself was later destroyed, but subsequent exhumations after the conflict, when international investigators were allowed back into Kosovo, recovered the bodies of 54 of the victims. The post mortem examination revealed the cause of death in 98 percent of the cases was related to gun-shot wounds. We have on the screen a map of Bela Crkva. I indicated that the village itself was destroyed. You can see on the map the left, the building intact is on the 11th of March, 1999, and that on the right is on the 2nd of April, 1999. You can see the tremendous devastation in the area. I should point out that the map, the second map, is reversed 180 degrees, but it is not difficult to identify where we are. If we look at the river, if we use as the point of reference the river, that is, the dark semi-circular line to the right of the map and the white building in the centre of the map, you can see that the -- both maps depict the same place at different times, one with the buildings and the other with the devastation. Thank you. Next we could move on to Mala Krusa. This is a neighbouring village of Bela Crkva in Orahovac. The map just indicates where it is in Kosovo. On the same day, a few kilometres from Bela Crkva in Mala Krusa, the forces of the FRY and Serbia also attacked that village. The villagers fled into the nearby forest from where they could see the attackers looting and burning their houses. The next morning, on the 26th of March, the Serbian forces located many of the villagers on the outskirts of Mala Krusa. They ordered the women and children to leave and to go to Albania, the common theme. They detained and searched the men and older boys and robbed them of their valuables and identity documents. The forces of the FRY and Serbia then forced the men and older boys into a nearby cow-shed and began firing upon them with machine-guns. They then set the shed on fire. Approximately 100 were killed in that massacre, and we obviously will not have forensics for that, or forensic reports for that site as the victims were burnt in the fire. If we could move on next to Suva Reka, and the map here shows where it is in Kosovo. Also on the 26th of March, the same day as the attack in Bela Crkva and Mala Krusa in Orahovac, policemen from the Suva Reka police station surrounded the Berisha family compound in Suva Reka town, the largest town in the municipality, and ordered the occupants out of one of the houses. Four men were killed on the spot and the remaining family members, mostly the elderly women and children, ran and took refuge in a coffee shop or a pizzeria. There they were fired upon by the police. Explosives were also thrown into the shop where the victims were. I would like to show you an aerial photograph, if you will, of the area. You will see the arrow showing you where the house -- the houses of the Berishas were, where the police station is; and if you look in the middle of the map, you will see a straight line coming down and ending at a structure beside three vats. That is where the pizzeria is, or was located. So you get an idea of the location of these premises, notably that the police station is basically across a road about 150 metres from where these women and children were massacred. After the massacre, probably in order to conceal the crime and the blood that remained in the pizzeria, the shop was -- fire was set to the shop. If we look on the screen, we can see what the destroyed coffee shop looked like after the bodies were removed and it was set ablaze.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You will see the pockmarks of automatic weapons on the walls. And there was damage from the explosives that were thrown inside. The women and children and the elderly had sought refuge in the shop, but at least 47 of them were killed inside that shop, 15 women and 17 children included. The police and members of the civil defence arranged then for the disposal of the bodies. The bodies of the victims were thrown in the rear of two trucks which drove off in the direction of the town of Prizren. Unbeknown to the assailants, not all were killed. Amazingly there were three survivors - two little children -- or two women and a small child who pretended to be dead and was thrown into the truck. While the truck was driving, they managed to escape by crawling out from among the bodies and jumping off the truck, and we will hear live testimony from some of those survivors. You will also hear about where these bodies of these women and children were eventually found, where they ended up. Remains of the Berisha family killed on that day were found in two different locations. I have just been advised -- Your Honours, I've just been advised that it might well be time for the break, to facilitate the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was watching and waiting for you to come to a convenient point to pause. This obviously is it. We must, for those who are new to the trial process here, break at about one and a half hours for half an hour to allow the recording machines, visual and sound, to be rewound and reordered and to allow those who are providing the interpretation to have a break, and we will establish regular approximate times for those breaks as the trial progresses. At about an hour and a half, those breaks will be established. So we must adjourn now for the first of them, resuming at 11.00. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, if it pleases you. When we last broke off, I was discussing what happened to the bodies of the members of the Berisha family that were killed at Suva Reka and loaded in a truck, or in two trucks and driven off towards Prizren that day. Your Honours, you will hear that remains of some of the family members that were killed that day were found in two different locations. Some were exhumed at a military firing range located just outside the town of Prizren. Secondly, remains later identified by DNA analysis as belonging to some 24 Berisha family members, as well as a foetus - one of the victims of the massacre was pregnant, I should inform the Court, so a foetus was also found - they were found in a clandestine grave-site at the police training centre, the training centre for the SAJ, the Special Elite Police Force of the Serbian MUP at Batajnica near Belgrade, in Serbia. This was in 2001. It appears, Your Honour, from examination of the forensic reports that some of the persons who were initially buried at the firing range in Prizren in Kosovo were disinterred, removed from there, and reburied at the SAJ firing range at Batajnica, near Serbia. Now, there is much significance in that, Your Honours, and I want to pause to show you a graphic that will enable you to understand more clearly the distances we are talking about. It's easy to understand for those familiar with the geography of the Netherlands and The Hague. You will see that the distance from Suva Reka to Batajnica in Serbia proper is just about the distance from The Hague to Luxembourg, a distance of almost 300 kilometres. How did these bodies get from Suva Reka to Belgrade, some 285 kilometres away? And not just to Belgrade, not just to any piece of ground, but to police property, to the police training ground, the Special Elite Units training ground that had strictly limited access? Why would dead Albanian civilians, women and children, be taken away and hidden there like that? And who had the means and opportunity to do that? And what motive was involved that would take one to go to such logistical lengths during a state of war, that involved so much resources not only in Kosovo but in Serbia property, resources of manned trucks and fuel to accomplish that task? This evidence, Your Honour, reflects guilty knowledge, guilty knowledge that these were the victims of murder and the murders were committed in the course of a criminal enterprise. More, a little bit more on the mass graves later on, if I may, Your Honour. If I could move on to the crime site of Podujevo. On the map you will see Podujevo is a town on the other side of Serbia, the north of Serbia -- I beg your pardon, the north of the province of Kosovo. On the 28th of March, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked Podujevo, which is a small town, and began expelling Kosovo Albanian civilians from their homes. A unit that was incorporated into the police, into the special SAJ, known as the Scorpions, entered the village and entered a house in the village and ordered a group of 19 women and children from the Bogujevci, Duriqi, sorry, and Llugaliu families to gather in the courtyard. They beat and shot at these people. At least 14 members of these families were killed and others were seriously wounded in the shooting. Again, some were fortunate enough to survive, and two survivors of that massacre, who were children at the time, as well as one member of the police unit that perpetrated this assault will testify at this trial. Again, this map indicates the local police station was just a couple -- less than a couple hundred yards away. Significantly, the accused was informed of this notorious crime and the unit was withdrawn from Kosovo. There were some, what we say are, token proceedings that were carried out. Nobody was punished. And some two weeks later, the unit that committed this massacre, were again redeployed into Kosovo by this accused and again featured in the commission of war crimes against the Kosovo Albanian population. If we could move to the municipality of Djakovica. Djakovica town is the capital of Djakovica municipality, and one site there is 157 Milos Gilic Street. On the night of the 1st to 2nd of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia launched an operation against the Qerim -- I'm sorry, Qerim district in Djakovica town. Over the period of several hours they forcibly entered houses of Kosovo Albanians, killed the occupants, and then set the houses on fire. During that night, Serb policemen attacked a house at 157 Milos Gilic Street. A group of 20 civilians, 19 of them women and children, having heard of the approaching Serbian forces, sought shelter in the basement of that house. The policemen forced them out of the basement and into the house. They shot the civilians and set fire to the house. Your Honours will hear the harrowing account of the sole survivor, who was only 10 years old at the time, who witnessed the killings of his family and neighbours. He managed to escape by pretending to be dead and jumped out of a window once the police had left. Next, I'd like to discuss the Izbica massacre. Izbica is a town in the -- toward the centre of Kosovo, in the Srbica municipality. There, on the 20th of March, forces of the FRY and Serbia began heavy weapons firing on several villages in the area of Izbica. As many as 45.000 people fled the attack and gathered in a field near Izbica. On the 20th of March, the forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded these displaced Kosovo Albanian civilians. The women and children were ordered to leave and told to go to Albania. Two disabled elderly women seated in a trailer were unable to walk. Serb forces set fire to the trailer and burned these two women alive. Again, the men were separated from the women and children and then divided into two groups. One group was taken toward the woods and a stream where are they were told to kneel down and then the Serb forces began shooting them. The second group was marched off in another direction and made to line up before they, too, were shot. Miraculously, there were survivors from both these mass executions, and you will hear live from at least one of them. Over 116 men were killed that day in Izbica. A local doctor, Liri Loshi, who will testify here, filmed the bodies for identification, and you'll see that in full later in the evidence. Local villagers gathered the dead and buried them, but they didn't stay buried for long. Dr. Loshi's video had been broadcast internationally. It appears that the response of the Serb media was that the video was fake, in effect denying that any massacre had occurred. At any rate, between mid-May and the 3rd of June, 1999, the Izbica killing victims were disinterred of what had previously been presumed to be their final resting place. I have aerial photos of the area. In the one before Your Honours, you'll see in the photo on the left, the 9th of March, there's an area, a rectangular-shaped area on the top of the photograph where you'll see that there are no graves. The photograph to the right, 15th of April, 1999, shows that graves had been built. There are rows of graves there. It's probably clearer if one looks at the next graphic. That's it. Thank you. This shows the graves, that a graveyard was there, 7th of May, on the left, and on the right there were more graves added. This is just a blow-up of the first photo -- photograph, aerial photograph. And if we could look at the third aerial photograph. Again, this shows on the left the rows of graves, 15th of May, and on the right, the photograph of the 3rd of June shows a dark spot. No more graves. The graves had been disinterred, clearly, it is our submission as a result of the international broadcast of Liri Loshi's videos of these dead persons. On the 27th of June, 1999, an international forensic teams entered Kosovo. A French forensic team examined the site at Izbica. They found no bodies in the areas where the greaves had been, but they did find evidence of human remains having been buried there at some time in the recent past. An investigations showed later that on the 1st and 2nd of June, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia had returned to the Izbica area and removed these bodies from the graves. Later on Serb authorities in 2001 and 2002, when, as it will become clear in the evidence, there was a different government in Serbia, the authorities admitted that they had removed the bodies. The bodies were indeed removed and there were some, it is submitted, token forensic analysis, where the Prosecution at the appropriate time will urge on this Court that the efforts in response of the international broadcast were merely token because, again, the Court will hear evidence as to what became of these bodies after they had been disinterred. In 2001, some 20 of the victims from the Izbica massacre were identified from human remains that were discovered in another clandestine mass grave at another police training ground at a place called Petrovo Selo in eastern Serbia, that is, outside of Kosovo, in Serbia proper, near the border with Romania. So, indeed, Your Honour, had the disinterment been for proper investigative purposes, these remains would not have been found, it is our submission, and we would urge later on, at a clandestine mass grave-site, hundreds of miles from where the massacre was committed. This was in 2001. So this is again evidence of an attempt to cover up a gross crime. It suggests guilty knowledge on the part of those involved in the cover-up. Like the Suva Reka situation, the persons were acting under the authority, and I mean the persons involved in these cover-ups were acting under the authority of this accused. They actually disinterred the victims of the massacres and travelled -- transported them some 250 miles to conceal them in Petrovo Selo. The last killing site - as I mentioned, today I will not go through all of them - that I would like to discuss briefly is Meja. Meja is a town in Djakovica, to the south-west of Kosovo, or maybe closer to the central west, if I may call it that, of Kosovo. In that municipality, on the 22nd -- 27th of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia began a large-scale operation in the area of Erenik and Trava River Valleys. On this map here, this topographical map, you can see both of the river valleys. Those river valleys had many villages occupied or populated by Kosovo Albanians, going right up towards the north. That's the upper part of the photograph. You will see a red dot in the middle of the map. That's Djakovica town, and you will see the pointer, the blue pointer, to the Erenik River. Right at the end of that pointer, where the arrow is, that is the vicinity of where the town of Meja and Korenica, the towns, the twin towns of Meja and Korenica are located. Kosovo Albanians began fleeing southward, down the mountain, down the river valleys from their villages; and several convoys were formed. In the vicinity of Meja, forces of the FRY and Serbia detained and separated hundreds of Kosovo Albanian men from the fleeing convoys. And you shall hear evidence, Your Honours, that many, many of them, were summarily executed and that senior members of the police were involved in participating in those executions. According to international organisations which compiled data, which will be tendered into evidence, over 344 men were not seen alive again. Two years later, about 300 of these men, who were removed from the convoys while attempting to flee down the hill, were identified by way of DNA analysis in human remains found at the mass grave-site inside the police grounds, again at Batajnica. And there is, again, a map similarly indicating to you the distance one would have to travel to take these bodies and hide them. It involved a significant amount of arrangement, a significant amount of logistics and coordination, not only of the police in Kosovo but also of the police in Serbia proper, and that is indicative, Your Honours, that somebody of the accused's rank and position, with command authority over the entire police in Serbia and Kosovo, would have been involved in orchestrating this scheme to remove these bodies. Your Honours, before I move on from the killing sites, I'd like to say a few more words about the mass graves. These mass graves were found in Serbia starting in 2001, after a newspaper report was published that during the war in 1999 one of the trucks that were conveying the bodies from Kosovo to Serbia proper had been in an accident and had ran off the road into the Danube River. This was published in early 2001 and led to an investigation in which the mass graves were found. This investigation involved the participation of many international organisations, including this Tribunal. Overall, the remains of approximately 800 Kosovo Albanians were identified through DNA analysis from the human remains in the mass graves, three mass graves, unearthed in Serbia in 2001. About one-half of them are not among the victims listed in the schedules to the indictment, but they are Kosovo Albanians that were reported killed or disappeared in Kosovo from places and at times where, according to the evidence to be tendered, there were ongoing expulsions of Kosovo Albanians. Evidence from several witnesses will show that this accused played a major role in orchestrating and organising the concealment of the bodies of the Kosovo Albanian victims in Serbia. Among these witnesses is a senior police officer who will testify that the accused personally ordered him to arrange trans-shipment of bodies of Kosovo Albanians that were in a refrigerator truck that was found abandoned in the Danube River. As I indicated, apparently the driver had been in an accident and had driven away -- driven off the road into the river. These bodies, the evidence will show, were taken to the SAJ training ground in Batajnica. Another witness, an SAJ officer who worked at the ground, will testify that he was ordered by the accused to receive and bury truckloads of corpses transported to the site, and that over a period of 20 days, from early April 1999, there were about six occasions when, on orders of the accused, he received truckloads of bodies to be buried at Batajnica. One -- another former police officer, senior police officer, will testify as to investigations into these mass graves, what the accused said and significantly did not say when he was confronted with the information of his role in these clandestine burials, and also of his flight and disappearance when he was informed that he would be officially interrogated in respect to these mass graves. Indeed, that officer will testify that his investigations revealed that sometime in the early part of the conflict there was a meeting in Belgrade involving Messrs. Milosevic, the MUP Minister Stojiljkovic, the Head of the State Security Department Markovic, and this accused, where the issue as to what is called "cleaning" or "clearing the battlefield" was discussed. And this accused suggested the removal of the bodies. If I may pause just to review, I think I might have misspoken. The Minister Stojiljkovic ordered the accused to make arrangements for the clearing of the battlefield, which is the disposal of these bodies, and the investigations of this officer also revealed that at a collegium of the Minister of the Interior, this accused deputied and instructed one Dragan Ilic, who is also named as a co-conspirator, or member of the JCE, Dragan Ilic, to make provisions for the criminal police from Belgrade to assist in the disposal or the concealment of the bodies of civilians that were murdered in Kosovo. So you will hear from these witnesses that the persons involved at the high level in clearing the bodies used the apparently innocuous term or expression for their doing, "clearing the battlefield" or "cleaning the battlefield"; and this expression in certain context may refer to legitimate activity when there are battles, that is, clearing the ground after a battle of unexploded ordinance, dead animals, dead persons, and the like. But when it was used in this context, Your Honours, they were not referring to the casualties of war or anti-terrorist action that may be urged later on. They were referring to the cover-up of mass murder. Yet the architects of this cover-up failed miserably. The eye-witness to these killings will testify that the people were executed en masse. In addition, you will hear the testimony of Dr. Jose Barybar, a forensic anthropologist, that the vast majority of the victims whose remains were recovered from the mass graves in a state susceptible to forensic examination had been killed by gun-shot wounds inflicted in circumstances where they were not or unlikely to have been involved in combat. The evidence from the mass graves, it is the Prosecution's submission, proves that the murders were the result of a widespread and systematic campaign. The Office of Missing Persons and Forensics, the OMPF, of the United Nations Mission in Kosovo gathered data on persons reported missing in Kosovo during the indictment period. This will be submitted in evidence. The reports include the locality and the municipality of the disappearance or death of each person and the date of the disappearance. The distribution, according to the locality of death or disappearance of the victims that were identified from the remains of the mass grave, is depicted in the map now before you of Kosovo, the larger green circles indicating where there were more concentrations or a higher number of the disappearances were reported. You will see to the left-hand bottom of the map there is a -- the Meja area. I should point out that in the middle of the map, to the south, you will see Suva Reka. Due to my oversight, the marking, the green marking for Suva Reka is not there, but there ought to be a green dot for Suva Reka because, as you will recall, there were about 30 bodies from the Suva Reka massacre that were recovered in Serbia. But you will see the spread as to where these people came from. All over Kosovo. Not from one place but all over Kosovo. You will also note when you receive the evidence and review it that the spread was over time. Meja was toward the latter part of April, that's the Meja massacre. Suva Reka was the 25th of March, and it spreads right throughout that period. And you will ask yourself, or it is submitted that you're entitled to ask yourself as to how could this have been coordinated and achieved if it was not a part of a systematic organised campaign. We say, Your Honours, that the collection and disposal of the remains of so many victims killed at disparate places and at different times during the indictment period demonstrates that the accused participated in planning and organising not only the concealment of the bodies and the cover-up of the murders, but it also supports the short inference that this accused was a leading figure in coordinating a widespread and systematic campaign of violence against the Kosovo Albanians. You may, Your Honours, conclude, after hearing the evidence led, that as police chief for all of Serbia, his role was indispensable in facilitating the crimes, as without him it is hard to conceive how this scheme involving police officers from different areas in Kosovo and in Serbia as well could have even been attempted. The Prosecution will make the appropriate submissions as to what could be made of what we might term the "bodies" evidence in due course. Before moving on to discuss the deportation sites, I direct your attention, Your Honours, with your leave, to another matter worth mentioning in regard to the killings. Based on rough mathematical calculations, the number of named, identified victims from the specific killings that are listed in a schedule to the indictment total 838 individuals, mostly men. This is consistent, of course, with the evidence that oftentimes the men were taken away from the convoys and murdered. Of that total, however, 53 were children under the age of 16 years; 41 were women; 92 were elderly men, over the age of 65 years. We suggest that these are not what you might expect to see from a legitimate campaign against armed terrorists. In regard to the deportations, as I indicated earlier, where there were these murders, there were refugees; there were deportations. But if I may touch briefly on four of the deportation municipalities or four of the deportation sites. Before you, Your Honours, is a map showing many of the areas from where the -- from where people were deported. I should point out that persons were deported, obviously, from all parts of Kosovo, but these are some of the major areas. The evidence will show a pattern of conduct by forces of the FRY and Serbia which supports the inference that this was a widespread and systematic attack directed against the civilian Kosovo Albanian population; that it was well-planned and coordinated from above, and that its objective, at least one of its primary objectives, was to modify the ethnic balance in Kosovo in order to maintain Serb control. Generally speaking, in the eastern part of Kosovo, as you will see from the upcoming map, the forces of the FRY and Serbia drove the people, the Kosovo Albanians, to the south, towards Macedonia. In the western side of the province, the people, the refugees, tended to be pushed towards Albania, and you will see on the map here some border crossings that no doubt in the course of the evidence you will become familiar with, Cafa Morines, Cafa Prusit, Djeneral Jankovic, being some of the more significant ones. There were five primary border crossing points that no doubt you will become family with.
