As I indicated earlier, border crossings were under the control of the border police from the Public Security Department led by the accused, and these police, they were involved in mistreating the Kosovo Albanian refugees and taking away their identification documents. If I may turn to Pec. In the town of Pec, in Pec municipality, forces of the FRY and Serbia went from house to house, forcing the Kosovo Albanians to leave their homes. In the course of this process, persons were killed and many houses were set on fire. Serb soldiers and police directed the civilians to the town centre where those without their own vehicles were forced to get on buses and trucks. They were then driven to Prizren and towards the border with Albania. The Kosovo Albanians were then forced off the buses and trucks and directed to walk the last 15 kilometres to Albania. At the border, before leaving Kosovo, they were ordered to turn over their identity papers to the forces of the FRY and Serbia. If we could look at Prizren municipality for the deportation routes from Prizren. You can also see the people from Meja and Korenica, many of them went through Prizren and from there to Albania. Beginning 25 March, forces of the FRY and Serbia began attacking villages in this municipality, forcing Kosovo Albanians from their homes and sending them to the Albania border. In the town of Prizren, beginning on the 20th of March, forces of the FRY and Serbia went from house to house ordering the Albanians to leave. They formed convoys and headed towards the border where many of them were assaulted and some of them were forced to make the last 15-kilometre part of the journey to the border on foot. Some were beaten and killed in that journey. And, again, as is a pattern, at the border, their identity documents were taken away. The same thing was repeated in Pristina. The map before Your Honours show the deportation sites from Pristina. Many of these people were put on trains, as we saw in the film, and taken to the various border crossings. The pattern in Pristina was the same. I don't think I need to go through it. The border crossings or the -- you'll see from the map that the persons who joined these convoys out of Pristina came from the surrounding districts, the areas surrounding Pristina, and, as usual, many of them were assaulted on their way and beaten, robbed, and killed, travel document taken away. Urosevac. Urosevac is the capital town of the Urosevac municipality. It's on your screen before you. Again, the people who had been forced out of their homes, the villagers from the surrounding villages or the villages surrounding the towns, would have been forced from their homes, as you can see from the convoy routes. They were marched off or forced to form convoys towards the town Urosevac, and from there towards the border to Macedonia, the border crossing to Macedonia. That point is Djeneral Jankovic border crossing. So I will not -- I don't think it is necessary to go into the details. The evidence will make it clear how these people were forced from their homes and directed, almost like cattle, towards these corridors to leave the country. As I indicated earlier, many times when the villages and the towns were surrounded, a path was always left open for people to flee, for people to leave, and in many cases the people before taken away on trains. The indictment, Your Honours, if I may move on, also charges the accused with persecutions and this includes the destruction of cultural sites and religious buildings. This destruction and the widespread destruction, I should call it, of Kosovo Albanian cultural structures and religious buildings is evidence, we say, Your Honours, of persecution on racial, political, and religious grounds. The evidence will show that many times during the deportations and the killings, the assailants also destroyed the mosques and other cultural sites of the Kosovo Albanians, intending that these people not return. You'll see scrolling through in front of you photographs of many of these destroyed structures. Much of this will be led in evidence and a number of witnesses will testify as to how these cultural sites were damaged or destroyed, including an expert on the subject, Andreas Riedlmayer. The evidence of all of these witnesses will say that not only were the crimes committed in a manner intended to discriminate against these people on racial and religious grounds, but there was an intention that the people who had been driven out were not expected or intended to return. And the eye-witness and expert evidence will also show that the damage was not done by NATO bombing, as might be asserted. It was not from the air but rather from the ground, by forces of the FRY and Serbia. The evidence, we submit, in total will lead you to the irrefutable conclusion that these religious and cultural sites were specifically targeted by the forces of the FRY and Serbia who were engaged in a campaign of persecution, as defined in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The evidence will further show, if I may move on to the additional liability of this accused under Article 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal, the evidence will show that none of the crimes charged here were properly investigated during the time when the accused occupied his position as chief of the police, nor were the perpetrators punished. This general impunity for serious violations of humanitarian law against ethnic Albanians in Kosovo did not exist because there were problems in the courts that were functioning during or after the conflict. On the contrary, the civilian courts worked normally during the conflict and thereafter. Nevertheless, impunity prevailed for the crimes we are dealing with in this trial, the serious crimes committed against Kosovo Albanians by the Serbian police. The murders charged in the indictment were massacres on a massive scale and must have been notorious when they were committed; yet at that time, no necessary appropriate actions were taken to punish the offenders. We expect to prove during this trial that the widespread persecution, deportation, murder, mistreatment, rape, and destruction of property committed against the Kosovo Albanians was not a matter of serious concern for the police authorities. There was no meaningful, substantive effort to fully investigate such matters or to see the MUP perpetrators of such crimes punished. The occasional rare investigation, usually when something received some international attention, that did take place were superficial, and the perpetrators remained unknown, unlocated, uncharged, and unpunished, at least during the time when this accused occupied the position up to 2001. The evidence will lead -- the evidence we will lead on the investigations into the massacres at Izbica and Podujevo will show that these were just token efforts. Impunity for the crimes concerned in this indictment went hand in hand with attempts to conceal these crimes. At different crime sites described before, the perpetrators attempted to dispose of the corpus delicti, the human remains and bodies of the murdered victims, by dynamiting or blowing up houses in which the massacres had taken place, setting them on fire, and otherwise hiding corpses. This sort of cover-up not only occurred in respect to the sites we described before, but also in respect to other sites like Kacanik, for example. Finally, the evidence will show that in many cases, crimes committed against Kosovo Albanians were not only tolerated but were ordered to be committed by superior officers of the direct perpetrators. In the course of this trial, you will hear live testimony from witnesses, policemen, who experienced this themselves. We say, Your Honours, respectfully, that this evidence will prove responsibility of the accused under Article 7(3) of the Statute. We say that the accused had effective control over the police perpetrators, meaning the material ability to prevent or punish the commission of the offences. He had the material ability to enforce discipline among the policemen he deployed to Kosovo and to effect the prosecution and punishment of perpetrators by virtue of his police -- by virtue of his position as chief of the police. By virtue of that position, his de jure and de facto powers, it was within his power and authority to take measures that would have prevented the crimes or punished the perpetrators. We will lead documentary evidence, Your Honours, of the accused exercising his authority over the forces in Kosovo as chief of the police. I indicated earlier an example of one such order issued by the accused in respect to his forces in Kosovo, and this one is one of the 21st of March, where he deploys various units. Firstly, he -- this is an order to all the SUP chiefs, including the SUP chiefs in Kosovo, signed by the accused and dated the 21st of March - several of these, as I indicated, will be tendered into evidence - where he deploys units in Kosovo and orders what is to be done to accommodate and to enable these units to operate in Kosovo, and these orders issued by the accused in respect to his units in Kosovo were in mandatory terms. These were orders that he was issuing. So he had effective control over these units. The evidence, Your Honours, will also show that the accused knew, or had reason to know, that serious violations of international humanitarian law, just described, were committed by MUP forces or forces subordinated to them or incorporated into them and operating in Kosovo. He had specific information in his possession which put him on actual notice of the Podujevo massacre, for example, including a report that was addressed to him, and yet his response was token and inadequate. He also knew of the criminal propensity of certain elements within the MUP. Despite his superior position and his material ability to take necessary measures and his knowledge, he failed to prevent and punish these gross crimes. And that is why we say he is responsible under Article 7(3). If I may make some general remarks before I close, Your Honours. The case against the accused will be complex. It will be broad in scope, reflecting the nature of the charges; and yet it will be detailed, as criminal cases must be, with specific features of the evidence are required to be explored in depth. As the accused was a member of a joint criminal enterprise, as we allege, it is necessary to tender much of the evidence previously presented in the trial of his co-indictees, or his former co-indictees, in order to show the complete picture. As was discussed recently, we have applied that some of the evidence that was introduced in previous -- in the previous trial be received in writing under the rules of this Tribunal. However, we will bring some witnesses here, or we propose to bring some witnesses here, and for many of them, this will be the third time they are coming to The Hague to testify at this Tribunal; and in many cases we ask the Court to understand that it involves some considerable degree of stress for some people to travel here to recount much of these harrowing experiences, and to some degree witness -- what we term "witness fatigue" may set in. We are grateful for the patience of these witnesses and sacrifice that many of them make in the interests of justice. The Prosecution will also tender a significant amount of documents. I won't comment on these. Many of them will speak for themselves. Among the witnesses we intend to call are what we refer to as "insiders." These witnesses are former policemen or soldiers. They are former members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia who will testify about some of the crimes committed and also about the organisation and structure of the MUP and the role of the accused. Some of them, Your Honours, are fully cooperative and speak from a desire to clear their conscience and to demonstrate that it is not the Serbian nation, it is not the spirit of the Serbian people that caused these crimes but rather individuals, individuals who are responsible for these gross crimes against humanity, persons in leadership positions that incited and orchestrated them. Other insiders are not so cooperative, as one can imagine, and we will seek the assistance of this Trial Chamber in order to ensure their attendance. I have already introduced Ms. Kravetz, to my right. Earlier today Ms. Gopalan was here, and yesterday Mr. Neuner was here. They will be actively involved Your Honours will be happy to know, in the presentation of these case, and therefore you will not be seeing me much of the time. I'm sure that will come as some relief to Your Honours. There are other lawyers on the team and they may also take part in some of the work here in court, and you may become familiar with them over time. They are Ms. Silvia D'Ascoli, Ms. Tove Nilson, and Mr. Eliott Behar. I wish to thank all of them for their work in the preparation of the case and later its presentation. I also wish to thank my colleague Mr. Tom Hannis, who was integral in the preparation of this case and also this opening address. Your Honours, we are honoured to appear before this Chamber and will endeavour to present the Prosecution's case in the highest traditions of fairness and professionalism. So, Your Honours, I come back to the narrative. So why, why did these crimes happen? The short and simple answer is that the participants in the JCE were fed up with the Kosovo problem, and they were determined not to yield Kosovo in spite of the will of the majority Kosovo Albanians. For years they had tried various measures but without success. The Serbs were losing the demographic game in Kosovo, and it would only get worse. Efforts to deal with the problem through legislation and increasingly discriminatory measures did not work. Use of force by the police and then the military did not work. It made the situation worse. More and more Kosovo Albanians abandoned the notion of non-violent civil resistance and turned to the KLA and a programme of violent resistance. By the time the conflict started, the decision had been made -- the conflict in March 1999, the decision had been made and the forces put into place to finally make a significant change in the ethnic balance in Kosovo. So the victims of the crimes enumerated in the indictment were not collateral damage from a conflict between the KLA and the FRY, nor from the NATO bombings. This was not a series of coincidences, nor was it simply the sad and unavoidable consequence of a legitimate anti-terrorist campaign by the forces of the FRY and Serbia. This was a plan, directed from above, coordinated by the accused and other members of the JCE, using the forces under their command and control to bring the objective of the JCE into reality. All the evidence considered together can only lead to the inference and the solid conclusion that these crimes were part of a common plan. As you listen to the evidence unfold, Your Honours, over the next few months, you will undoubtedly be struck by some key factors which I ask you to bear in mind from the outset, and these include the nature of the armed conflict beginning on the 24th of March, that is, a coordinated, widespread, systematic nature of the attacks all over Kosovo, and the pattern, the same pattern happened at practically the same places in different municipalities over Kosovo. The number of children, women and elderly victims who were obviously not KLA fighters or terrorists. The efforts to conceal the crimes, particularly taking the great logistical pains and using precious resources to transport the bodies hundreds of kilometres away to mass graves in Serbia proper. The attacks also predictably included verbal abuse on ethnic grounds and the confiscation and destruction of identity documents. You will see that as a common theme throughout the evidence. At the conclusion of our case, the Prosecution submits that the body of evidence tendered will leave the Trial Chamber with no reasonable doubt that the accused is guilty as charged on each count of the indictment. Your Honours, my colleagues and I look forward to presenting our case to you, and I thank you very much for your kindness and permission in allowing me to speak today, may it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Djordjevic, as foreshadowed yesterday, this is an occasion when it is open under the rules for an opening statement to be made on the part of the Defence. Is it desired to do that at this stage of the trial, or is it proposed to wait until the actual opening of the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are not going to do that this time. We are going to do that when we start the Defence case. We should just like to ask the Trial Chamber to allow our client to make a brief statement today, in accordance with Rule 84 bis, of course, if you believe that this would be proper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification, Mr. Djordjevic. We have about 25 minutes left on the present tapes. Is your client's statement one that would conclude in that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced that that time will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being the case, then, and in view of your indication that the formal Defence opening will be delayed until the commencement of the Defence case, the Chamber would now allow the accused the opportunity to speak, address the Chamber, about matters relevant to this prosecution. It will be appreciated that we are concerned with the merits of this trial and the evidence to be led. We are not concerned with issues of wider political significance in Serbia and other parts. So we would ask that to be borne in mind as the statement is given. Is it convenient at this point, Mr. Djordjevic, to say what it is you wish to place before the Chamber? You may, if you wish, speak while seated. It's up to you whether you prefer to stand or sit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, thank you for having allowed me to address you after the opening statement made by the Prosecution. The indictment charges me that as a member of the joint criminal enterprise I committed the gravest crimes against the civilian Albania population. The objective of this joint criminal enterprise was allegedly the modification of the ethnic balance in Kosovo and Metohija in order to ensure continued Serbian control over the province. I must admit that I find the indictment to be unclear in the part that sets out the goal of the joint criminal enterprise. First of all, the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija is an integral part of the Republic of Serbia, which together with the Republic of Montenegro made up the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Serbia had sovereign power --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I must ask you to speak more slowly. You are getting increasingly ahead of the people trying to translate and interpret. If you wouldn't mind just speaking more slowly, it will enable them to keep up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Thank you. Serbia had sovereign authority over its entire territory, so Serbia could not take any action in order to ensure allegedly continued control. No state authority is limited in time and all countries in the world exercise sovereign authority over their territory in an unlimited span of time. On the other hand, a modification of the alleged ethnic balance in Kosovo and the Prosecution case that the Serbs in Kosovo and Metohija were a minority population and that many of them considered Kosovo an integral part of Serbia, which is what the Prosecutor says in his pre-trial brief, obviously indicates the political position of the OTP that Kosovo and Metohija is not an integral part of Serbia or, rather, that Serbia did not have sovereignty over Kosovo and Metohija. It seems to me that this kind of indictment shows what its political objective is, and this proceeding should be a legal vehicle for the implementation of that goal. I was born in Koznica, the municipality of Vladicin Han, in 1948, where I lived with my parents and younger brother. After completing secondary school, I graduated from the law school of the University of Nis in 1971; and I got a job in the Ministry of Interior, MUP, in the Republic of Serbia, in the SUP of Zajecar. While completing my internship, I became an inspector for white-collar crimes, and I was in that position for over a year. Towards the end of 1975, I became a senior police inspector. I became Chief of the Division for Police Affairs in the Police Administration of the Republican SUP in Belgrade in February 1982. I spent around eight years doing that job and then for a year and a half I was Chief of the Inspectorate for Internal Affairs, monitoring legality in the work of the Republican SUP. From time to time in 1981, for several years I carried out duties of highest responsibility in the area of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija, starting with battalion commander, all the way up to the commander of the joint force or the federal SUP, Federal Secretary for Internal Affairs, and the head of the staff of the MUP for the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. Towards the end of 1991, I was appointed Chief of the Administration of the Police, and I held that position until 1997, when, after the murder of General Radovan Stojicic, Minister Stojiljkovic first appointed me Acting Chief of Public Security and a few months after that, I received a decision on my appointment as Chief of the RJB. Up until then and after that in public and state security, there was no longer acting heads. The appointments were for the position of chief immediately. As chief of the public security department of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, it was my duty, in keeping with the policy and decisions of the state organs and especially of the Minister of the Interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, to carry out measures within the scope of the powers vested in me and pursue the state policy that had been set. I cannot accept that the President of the FRY, the President of the Republic of Serbia, the Deputy Prime Minister of the FRY, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Serbia, the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the Commander of the Third Army of the VJ, and the Commander of the Pristina Corps of the VJ, and the Head of the SUP Staff of the Republic of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija and I, as Chief of the RJB of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, are all engaged in a joint criminal enterprise as we carried out the set policy of all the political and state organs of the country aimed at curbing terrorism. At the highest state level what was approved and planned was an anti-terrorist activity during 1998, as well as during the defence of the country, and it was not aimed against the Albania civilian population in Kosovo and Metohija or against any other civilian population. The objective was to free roads, neutralise actions of the terrorists, find and set free citizens who had been kidnapped, to establish public law and order, and ensure the personal and property-related safety of all citizens of Kosovo and Metohija. These activities were aimed against the terrorists who wished through violent means to have Kosovo and Metohija secede from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and they wanted to achieve that by any means. During the war they openly stood on the side of the aggressor and represented the aggressor's land force or ground force that was supposed to facilitate and make possible through their activities a land aggression against Serbia. The methods of the activities of the terrorists were reflected in attacks against the army and the police that carried out their duties as established by the constitution and law. Then also by kidnapping and killing Albanians who were loyal to the state, as well as through terrorising the non-Albania population, blocking and barricading roads. In less than a year, for no reason whatsoever, policemen, soldiers, innocent citizens, were killed and kidnapped in order to create an atmosphere of a reign of terror, lack of tolerance, and to give rise to interethnic conflicts, all with the aim of establishing a Republic of Kosovo and attaining the cessation of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija from the Republic of Serbia. Armed from Albania and by the powerful forces, through different forms of activity, Albanian extremists and terrorists resorted to all possible means, including the civilian population, in order to attain their goals, especially creating a semblance of a humanitarian catastrophe while accusing the state forces for excessive use of force and non-observance of human rights. There was no plan or order for acting against the civilian Albanian population in any form. The activity of the state forces did not have as its objective the persecution of the non-Albania -- of the Albanian civilian population, creating an atmosphere of fear and insecurity, destroying property, cultural and religious landmarks. Within the scope of our possibilities we took all possible measures in order to resolve crimes, find their perpetrators, irrespective of national, ethnic, racial, and religious affiliation. Like in any war, there were crimes, but they had not been planned, instigated or approved. And as for the crimes and criminals who were found, action was taken in accordance with the procedures set by law in keeping with the possibilities and circumstances that we faced at the time. One should not lose sight of the fact that many crimes were not reported, which made the work of the police even more difficult in terms of uncovering crimes and perpetrators. And then the withdrawal of the military and police forces from the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija in June 1999, after the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement, rendered impossible the further work of our organs in that territory. Population movements took place for several reasons, namely, fear from bombing, fear from conflicts with terrorists, fear from combat activities. And also the terrorists abused civilian population in order to create an apparent humanitarian catastrophe. There was no forced movement of the population, and the population that fled was rendered all possible aid and assistance within the scope of the possibilities then existing. The position that I held then did not permit me to make state level and political decisions that were within the powers of various organs in accordance with the constitution and law, and it was the Minister of the Interior who prescribed the procedure in terms of implementing decisions that belonged to the purview of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and the RJB within it. From 1981 onwards, after the demonstrations that were held in Pristina when the demand Kosovo should be a republic was voiced with a view to the violent secession of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija from the Republic of Serbia, the Federal Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia established a staff which continued to exist and function all the way up to the end of June 1999. When the top state organs adopted in 1998 a plan for combating terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija, the Minister of the Interior passed a decision setting the mandate, composition, and responsibility of the staff of the MUP for combatting terrorism in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The minister decided that in addition to the appointed leader and members of the staff, that also included members of the RJB and the RDB, the broader composition should have attached to it the chiefs of the secretariats of the interior centres and divisions of the RDB in the territory in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. The task of the staff was to plan, organise, and lead the work and engagement of organisational units of the ministry as well as sent and attached units in controlling and combatting terrorism in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In addition to that, the task of the staff was to plan, organise, channel, and bring together the work of the organisational units of the ministry in Kosovo and Metohija in carrying out more complex security-related tasks. For his own work, the work of the staff, and the state of security within the purview of the staff itself, the head of the staff is -- directly reports to the minister, and he reports to the minister about security incidents, measures taken, and the results of these measures. When the minister made his decision of the 16th of June, 1998, he decided that all previous decisions on the establishment of the staff of the MUP and the decisions on appointing the composition of the staff of the MUP that I made as Chief of the RJB shall become null and void. The minister had the authority to make such a decision on the basis of the Law on the Interior and other bylaws. And that was the only solution possible, in view of the fact that the staff brought together the work of both departments of the MUP. So it was only the minister who could have made such a decision and regulate in this way the work and responsibility of the organ that was established at the level of all of the MUP. I never reported to any state organ, or did I brief it on the situation, plans, and tasks related to the security situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and no one reported to me, as the Chief of the RJB, on the planning, organisation and implementation of anti-terrorist actions in Kosovo and Metohija at the time relevant to the indictment. In accordance with the minister's order, I stayed in the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija from July 1998 until the end of September 1998. In that period a plan was carried out for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija which had been adopted by the top state leadership on the basis of a plan that had been adopted by the Army of Yugoslavia, and the MUP of the Republic of Serbia took part in that, too. I assumed that due to the complexity and seriousness of the security-related and political situation in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the minister decided that I should be present while the plan for combatting terrorism was being carried out in 1998. The staff was in charge of the MUP forces and coordination and activity with the Army of Yugoslavia was implemented in accordance with the adopted plan of the VJ, while coordinating activities with the commander of the Pristina Corps. Due to the gravity of the political situation, the situation in Kosovo and Metohija was uppermost political issue in the country and that is why the top political officials of the FRY and the Republic of Serbia came to the area of Kosovo and Metohija, and they dealt with the functioning of the state organs there. By monitoring the situation in the field every day and carrying out the adopted plan for combatting terrorism, what was necessary was the exchange of information and communication between and among all state structures so that the intimidated, terrified population would see that the state did care and was resolute in terms of establishing normal communication and movement of citizens throughout the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the personal and property-related security of citizens, and to establish the normal functioning of the state while curbing the activities of the terrorist forces and terrorism as such. After the plan for combatting terrorism was being carried out, there was a normalisation of work and life in Kosovo and Metohija. Inter-ethnic confidence was re-established and all persons returned to their homes and places of residence. The Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement was signed after intense political negotiations, and then on the 25th of October, pursuant to an authorisation given to me by the Minister of the Interior, I signed agreements with John Byrnes and Klaus Naumann specifying the number of observation points, reducing the strength of the police force, and limiting the use of weapons of larger calibre. Once the police forces withdrew in accordance with the agreement, the terrorist forces exploited the pull-out and retook their previous positions, continuing their terrorist activity. After this period, I would only go to Kosovo and Metohija in the escort of the minister or members of the Republic of Serbia government, and this was only for a few times up until the end of June 1999. In early 1999, it was assessed that there was a possibility that there would be an aggression against the territory of Serbia, first through air-strikes, followed by a ground invasion of the NATO forces. In the Serbian MUP, preparations were made for the defence of the country and war plans were updated. I ran the Public Security Department in the same manner, regardless of where the organisational units were located, throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia, within the framework of the powers that were vested in me by the minister. I have to stress that in his decision of the 16th of June, 1998, the minister, within the mandate and the composition of the MUP Staff for combatting terrorism in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, brought together both departments of the MUP and made all decisions relating to the tasks, operation, flow of information, and responsibilities of the staff. In the course of the combat operations, regular security tasks that the Public Security Department carried out were carried out in accordance with the laws and regulations throughout the territory of the Republic of Serbia, and as for me I ran the department from Belgrade, taking care of its work throughout the territory of the republic. It was only the minister that was in charge of the anti-terrorist activities in the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija before and during the war. He decided within the MUP who and how would carry out tasks in Kosovo and Metohija in accordance with the state policy as it was set. I never heard either the minister or any top people issue any tasks that would call for crimes against the Albania civilian population, that would incite MUP personnel to commit crimes or to the effect that their crimes would be tolerated. Regardless of the difficult situation that the country found itself in, what was insisted on was the legality in the work and operation of the MUP and respect of human rights. And as for those members of the MUP who violated the rules and regulations, disciplinary and criminal proceedings were instituted against them, with a special emphasis placed on the treatment of civilians and provision of humanitarian aid. Regular security duties were carried out in the same manner as we had done them before the war but in conditions that were substantially more difficult. We complied with the law and the regulations that were passed during the state of war. In light of the severe destruction caused by air-strikes, I had to take measures to eliminate the consequences, to ensure the swift and efficient operation of the MUP organs, and the coordination of the work with other relevant organs, primarily in an effort to attend the scenes of air-strikes as soon as possible; to have the first responders there as soon as possible, primarily the fire-fighting teams, and then other services who were there to assist the victims; and to carry out on-site investigation and to document the consequences of the air-strikes, determining the number and identity of the casualties, both killed -- those who were killed and who were wounded, recording the destroyed facilities, and so on. Difficulties experienced in communications made it even more difficult to carry out these tasks and required swift reactions throughout the territory of the republic. Throughout this time of the war, the headquarters of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and of the RJB was located in Belgrade, but the locations where our job was actually done changed all the time because of the air-strikes. Regular security work in all organisational units went on in a unified way, and reports about security incidents that I received every day did not contain any information or data about anti-terrorist activities. I did not take part in the drafting of the plans for combatting terrorism. I was not aware. I did not receive any information about where those activities would take place, and I did not take part in their implementation in the time relevant for the indictment. The call-up, the training of the regular and reserve force, dispatching units to Kosovo and Metohija, their billeting and board, these are regular tasks that the appropriate administration in the RJB is charged with, or sections and divisions within various SUPs. But those activities don't have anything to do with the planning, control, or actual implementation of anti-terrorist activities. Disciplinary proceedings were carried out in accordance with the regular procedure, and this was something that the Public Security Department did. It was one of its regular tasks. No paramilitary units were ever drafted into the reserve force of the MUP of Republic of Serbia. It was only individuals, in accordance with the relevant laws. The reception was carried out by the police administration in accordance with the military offices and local SUPs. I first learned about the truck with the bodies from the chief of the SUP in Bor, not knowing how the truck got to be in the Danube, where it had come from, or who had organised the transport. After receiving this information, I thought that the regular police crime investigation had to be carried out, in accordance with the law, and this is what I insisted on in my conversation with the chief of the SUP in Bor. However, having received additional information, and in light of the fact that the local SUP could not do this in accordance with the procedure, I informed the minister about all that and he took all the decisions that followed, and I relayed them to the chief of the SUP in Bor and to other persons who took part in the implementation of the orders from the minister. I could not effect the decisions that were made, and bearing the time when all this was going on, the state of war, the aggression, I could not leave my post, and I could not refuse to implement the orders that I received. After the change in the government in Serbia, I received reliable information from my close associates that my life was in danger. At the same time, I learned that the people who were now in government, after retirement, wanted to place me under arrest for reasons that were unknown to me; and they would quote the wrong-doings that I purportedly had done in the Milicionar Sports Association as a pretext. Bearing all this in mind, the facts that I just quoted, I left Serbia in 2001. The way I chose, I can see now, was the wrong one because I would have been able in talks with the state organs, with representatives and investigators of this Tribunal, to clear up my role and my actions and avoid the indictment against me. The indictment was issued in late 2003, more than two years after I had left Serbia. I am absolutely convinced of that because in the book published by former Chief Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte, I read that at a secret meeting held in the Netherlands on the 2nd of April, 2003, the Foreign Minister of Serbia, Goran Svilanovic and the Minister of the Interior, Dusan Mihajlovic spoke with Chief Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte about their continued cooperation and future indictments. On that occasion, the Minister of the Interior, Mihajlovic, said that the government of Serbia would be overjoyed if the Tribunal in The Hague would indict General Djordjevic. That's at page 195. When the indictment against me, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, and General Lukic was handed over, Zoran Zivkovic, the then Prime Minister of Serbia, this is what Carla Del Ponte says, refused to take receipt of the indictment, but when he looked at the names, he said, "Djordjevic, no problem." That's at page 205 of the same book. Your Honours, I hope that in the course of a fair trial, I will be able to prove that the allegations made by the Prosecution are unfounded. I did not have effective control over the MUP units that were active in the area of Kosovo and Metohija in the period relevant for the indictment. I did not know, I did not have reason to know, that my subordinates committed widespread crimes against the Albania population. I did not receive any information about punishable conduct of the MUP units. Within the limits of my power, I took legal action against the perpetrators of crime, and we also carried out preventive actions to prevent crimes. You also have to bear in mind the actual real-life situation at the time when all of this was going on and the actual capability for acting promptly. I'm sorry for all the victims in Kosovo and Metohija. I feel sorry for the families. I deeply sympathise with their pain. I would really wish to see this war, the war in Kosovo and Metohija, to be the last war ever waged there; and I would like to see all the problems being resolved by political means, by talks, and agreements. Thank you very much for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd be good enough to switch off your microphone. Thank you. It reduces, then, the humming. We have now given the accused the opportunity which he sought, allowed by the rules, to make a personal statement at this time and that has been recorded, and we have noted its content. That concludes the preliminary statement procedures for this trial. The next stage is for the actual evidence for the Prosecution to be led. Following that, of course, the Defence will have an opportunity to present its case in answer to the Prosecution evidence. Given the time now and the practicalities for the arrival and processing of witnesses, the Chamber proposes to adjourn now with a view to resuming tomorrow morning at 9.00 to commence the hearing of the evidence. Could I mention, in case there has been any confusion, that we are not able to sit on Thursday of this week. There is no courtroom available. One timetable that is available on the internet suggests that we are sitting. That is a mistyping. Another trial is, in fact, sitting at that time. So we will hear evidence tomorrow and then continue on Friday and then into next week. So we thank you, Mr. Stamp, for your opening statement, and we have heard the personal statement of the accused. We now adjourn and will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of January, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
